name: The Kingdom of Kongo
title: Social Hierarchy of the Kingdom of Kongo: From King to Enslaved
period: 1509–1665 (from Afonso I to the Battle of Mbwila)

tiers.name: The king
tiers.you: You were chosen for life from among the royal kin; you name the governors, keep the nzimbu shells that serve as money and pay the church, while rival branches of the royal family eye the throne.
tiers.kid: The king of Kongo ruled from the city of Mbanza Kongo and was chosen from the royal family.
tiers.rise: Election, not birth order, made a king, so any man of the royal kin with enough support could hope to reign: Álvaro I, not directly descended from a previous king, took the throne in 1568 and founded a new line. Kings could also fall in battle, as António I did at Mbwila in 1665.
tiers.why: The king of Kongo, the mwene Kongo or manikongo, was chosen for life by a small group of electors and senior officials from among the royal kin.

tiers.name: Royal kin and great nobles
tiers.you: As governor of a province, now styled duke or count, you name your clients to lower posts, collect the head tax and send part of it to the king, who can in principle dismiss you.
tiers.kid: Kongo’s great nobles governed its provinces, and some took Portuguese titles such as duke or count.
tiers.rise: Noble birth was needed, but office came from the king, who could in principle dismiss a governor; a province whose lord misbehaved could be raided by royal forces and some of its people enslaved.
tiers.why: The great nobles were the core of the mwissikongo, the ruling nobility of the capital: the royal kin, the electors and the governors of the great provinces, which had once been separate kingdoms.

tiers.name: Lesser nobles and officials
tiers.you: You hold one of the small lordships, or a post the king gave you for three years, live on revenue assignments from the head tax, and in war you join the heavy infantry, armed with swords and shields.
tiers.kid: Young nobles in Kongo went to royal schools and learned to read and write.
tiers.rise: Noble birth opened the way, but posts were held at a superior’s pleasure and renewed year by year, so a lord’s standing rose and fell with his patrons and his faction.
tiers.why: A wider nobility of lesser lords and office-holders lived in the capital and the provincial towns.

tiers.name: Clergy and lay teachers
tiers.you: You are one of the lay schoolmasters, recruited from the nobility and paid by the crown to teach the faith and lead worship where ordained priests are too few.
tiers.kid: Kongo had few priests, so Kongolese teachers, often nobles, taught people the Christian faith.
tiers.rise: The lay teachers came from noble families and were trained in the royal schools; a few Kongolese, such as Henrique, were ordained, but the priesthood stayed largely foreign.
tiers.why: From 1491, and above all under Afonso I, Kongo built a Catholic church of its own, paid for from royal revenues and from baptism and burial fees.

tiers.name: Free villagers
tiers.you: You farm with a village of one or two hundred people, pay the head tax in shells or goods and go to war as one of the archers of the levy; as one of the freeborn, you may not be enslaved unless convicted of a crime.
tiers.kid: Most people in Kongo were farmers who lived in small villages and paid taxes to their lords.
tiers.rise: Rank came by birth and office, and the schools that made nobles literate were not built for commoners. War, kidnapping or a court’s sentence could make a free villager a slave.
tiers.why: Most people of Kongo were free villagers.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You are one of the war captives settled around the capital to labour for the nobility; you can be bought and sold in Kongo’s markets, and the law that shields the freeborn does not cover you.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and made to work without pay; many were captured in wars.
tiers.rise: People entered slavery as war captives, by kidnapping or by a court’s sentence, which by the mid-17th century could fall on a convict’s whole family. Runaways from Portuguese Angola found refuge with the lords of southern Kongo, but the sources say little about how slaves inside Kongo won their freedom.
tiers.why: Slavery in Kongo was older than the Atlantic trade.
